title: Which Measure Separates Them?
scopeNote: This keeps the pairing and the prediction, which is the mechanism: the learner must commit to a measure before the scores are shown, because the intuitive answer, the lowest score, is frequently the wrong one. Two further profiles, the remaining pairings, and the running record of which measures earned their place stay in the longer version.
summary: Four fictional language profiles across four measures. The learner predicts which single measure will most separate a given pair, and the three pairings offered end on the case where the separating measure is neither profile's worst score.
learningObjectives: Explain why a measure is informative about a contrast rather than in general.
Identify the separating measure as the one with the largest gap, not the lowest score.
Explain why two profiles that are both poor on a measure cannot be told apart by it.
Explain what makes a score interesting: being out of line with the others rather than being low.
Recognise that a battery is chosen for the comparisons that need making.
interactionTypes: a two-profile pairing chosen from four
a prediction of the separating measure made before any score is shown
a paired bar chart with every gap marked and the largest highlighted
explanatory feedback that differs by whether the separator is also a lowest score
a curated sequence of three pairings ending on the instructive one
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout. A profile already chosen for one slot is disabled in the other and says so in its own label rather than only appearing greyed. The chart carries a description giving both scores and the gap for every measure and naming the largest and smallest, so the comparison is fully available as text. The two profiles are distinguished by vertical position and by an explicit key naming which bars are whose, and every gap is drawn as a marked span with the largest one labelled as such. Changing either profile clears the prediction rather than leaving a stale answer against new scores. Nothing is timed and there is no motion.
dataStatus: Four fictional profiles with invented scores. No real patient is described and nothing here is an assessment instrument.
simulationNotes: The scores are chosen so that the three offered pairings run easy, easy, then instructive. In the first two the largest gap falls on a measure that is one of the two profiles' lowest scores, which is the intuitive case. In the third, R against S, both profiles repeat badly, so repetition separates them by two points and is worthless, while naming, which is neither profile's lowest score, separates them by thirty-four. An earlier draft of these numbers had no such pairing at all, which made the feedback promise a case that did not exist; the sequence is curated rather than free precisely so the instructive pairing is actually reached.
readmeTopic: why the useful measure is the one the two candidates differ on, not the one either scores lowest on
